title: A Fun Way To Get Your Students To Follow Directions ections/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents a strategy for improving how well students follow multi-step directions: inserting a deliberately meaningless, often silly step into an otherwise ordinary set of instructions. He explains that breaking directions into concrete steps aids memory, and that adding something unusual—a dance move, a movie line, jumping jacks—sharpens attention and makes the sequence more memorable. He notes the strategy should be used sparingly, a couple times per week at most, or its novelty wears off. The broader point is that improving direction-following requires strategies that compel attention rather than repeated scolding or nagging about poor listening.
points: Following directions doesn't improve through frustration or repeated complaints—it improves through strategies that actively compel attention.
Breaking a direction into multiple concrete steps functions as memory 'hooks' that make the sequence easier to execute accurately.
Adding one silly, meaningless step (a dance move, a movie quote, jumping jacks) sharpens listening and boosts engagement.
Increasing the complexity and number of steps over time, rather than repeating simple directions, improves performance further.
The strategy should be used only a couple of times a week; overuse causes its novelty—and effectiveness—to wear off quickly.
quotes: Following directions doesn’t improve by harping on it. It doesn’t improve by making a fuss about it or showing your frustration over it.
One such strategy is to slip a meaningless step into your directions. It’s a bit unorthodox, to be sure, but it’s remarkably effective.
A meaningless step, especially if it’s silly or out of the ordinary, causes students to listen more intently to your directions and better visualize what you want them to do.
One of the keys to improving following directions is to increase the challenge.
It isn’t a strategy you’ll want to use all the time, however. The novelty will wear off quickly if you put it into practice more than a couple times per week.
